factions.label:
Progressive
Dem
factions.ideology: Progressive Caucus / Squad-adjacent. Left-leaning on economy, climate, healthcare. Many are senior members passing torch to younger generation.

factions.label:
Estab./Mod.
Dem
factions.ideology: Establishment centre-left / New Democrat Coalition / Blue Dogs. Centrist, pro-institution. Many leaving due to redistricting or declining appeal.
factions.members: Steny Hoyer, Jared Golden, Julia Brownley, Marc Veasey, Lloyd Doggett; Moulton, Haley Stevens, Pappas, Angie Craig (Senate); Swalwell (Gov, withdrew)

factions.label:
MAGA /
Hard-right GOP
factions.ideology: Trump loyalists / Freedom Caucus. Strong executive power, nationalism. Leaving partly due to frustration that Trump agenda is stalled in Congress.

factions.label:
America First /
Pro-Trump
factions.ideology: Pro-Trump but not Freedom Caucus. Support Trump agenda but outside hardline faction. Many seeking other offices to extend Trump-aligned agenda at state level.

factions.label:
Estab./Mod.
GOP
factions.ideology: Traditional establishment Republicans. Supports institutions, free trade, NATO. Often at odds with MAGA wing. Many are committee chairs stepping back.
factions.members: Elise Stefanik, Don Bacon, Darrell Issa, Buchanan, Mark Amodei, Daniel Webster, Burgess Owens, Jodey Arrington, McCaul, Newhouse

factions.label:
Independent
/ unclear
factions.ideology: Independent or ideologically unclear. Not formally aligned with a major caucus.

republican.name: Freedom Caucus
republican.ideology: Hard-right conservative. Anti-establishment. Willing to block leadership priorities.

republican.name: Republican Study Committee
republican.ideology: Broad conservative umbrella — largest House caucus. Pushes right-of-centre legislative agenda.
republican.outlook_label: Strong in safe seats; exposure in competitive districts

republican.name: Main Street Caucus
republican.ideology: Pragmatic, business-friendly Republicans. Moderate on immigration and social issues.
republican.outlook_label: Best-positioned if economy and tariffs stabilise

democrat.name: Progressive Caucus
democrat.ideology: Left-progressive. Medicare for All, Green New Deal, housing reform. Energising base in opposition.
democrat.outlook_label: Safe seats; energising base for potential 2026 wave

democrat.name: New Democrat Coalition
democrat.ideology: Centrist, pro-business Democrats. Technology, trade, and fiscal responsibility focus.
democrat.outlook_label: Key battleground — holds most swing-district D seats

democrat.name: Blue Dog Coalition
democrat.ideology: Conservative Democrats. Fiscally hawkish, moderate on social issues. Shrinking caucus each cycle.
democrat.outlook_label: Diminishing — caucus shrinking with each election cycle

democrat.name: Problem Solvers (D)
democrat.ideology: Bipartisan centrists. Work with Republican counterparts on compromise legislation.
democrat.outlook_label: Mixed — suburban districts trended blue in 2024

democrat.name: The Squad
democrat.ideology: Democratic socialist. Outsized national media presence. Galvanises progressive grassroots.
democrat.outlook_label: Safe — focus on expanding progressive wing nationally

midterms.context: First-term Clinton backlash. Republicans ran a unified Contract with America platform. Healthcare reform failure energised conservatives. Democrats lost 54 seats — largest loss since 1946.
Only second time since WWII that the president's party gained House seats in midterms. Republican impeachment of Clinton backfired. Booming economy and Clinton's 66% approval drove Democratic gains.

Rare midterm gain for the president's party. 9/11 national unity and Bush's 63% approval — highest any president heading into midterms — propelled Republicans to gains in both chambers. Democrats struggled to oppose the Iraq War.
key_factors: Highest pre-midterm presidential approval in modern history
Democrats divided on Iraq War authorisation

midterms.context: Iraq War dominated the election. Mark Foley congressional page scandal broke weeks before Election Day. Nancy Pelosi became the first female Speaker. Democrats flipped both chambers simultaneously for the first time since 1986.

Largest House swing since 1938 and the biggest midterm loss since Truman in 1946. 9.8% unemployment and ACA backlash fuelled the Tea Party movement. Census-year election gave Republicans sweeping redistricting power for a decade.

Second-term Obama drag. Oct 2013 government shutdown initially hurt Republicans but Democrats couldn't capitalise. Record-low turnout of 36.4%. Republicans flipped the Senate for the first time since 2006. Ebola fears and ISIS dominated the final weeks.

Democrats flipped 41 House seats driven by suburban college-educated women voters. The economy was strong but anti-Trump sentiment dominated. Republicans held and expanded Senate majority in a very favourable map — only 9 R seats vs 26 D seats up for election.

Expected red wave failed to materialise. Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade energised Democratic turnout especially among women and young voters. Republicans eked out a 9-seat House majority but significantly underperformed polling. Democrats gained a Senate seat in Pennsylvania.
